E447.text:
depth maps look plausible and correctly ordered, yet keep
2.7–9.3% error that is spatially structured: smooth bands
across the walls and floor of Classroom1 that correspond
to tilted or warped surfaces. This is the failure mode that
a precision metric would not see (section 4). Without the
oracle scale (table 7), the monocular errors are far larger.
Figure 4 compares the methods near the monocular
models’ native input, as deployed, i.e. without oracle
scale. libSGM at quarter resolution (6.1 ms) keeps about
1% error with holes at occlusions and in low-texture re-
gions; Fast-FoundationStereo at 512 × 768 is dense and
has 0.35–0.48% error.
The monocular models at their
native input have 11–39% error on these scenes: Depth
Anything V2 places almost all of Sword1 at the near end
of the depth range and MoGe-2-L at the far end, and the
error of Depth Anything 3 falls to 2.0–9.9% only with the
oracle scale.
6.5
FP16 fidelity
We compared every monocular TensorRT FP16 engine
with its FP32 PyTorch model on one scene. Depth Any-
thing V2 at native resolution differs by 0.10–0.17%, and
Base and Large at full resolution by 0.19% and 0.25%
(median relative depth difference).

E448.text:
Depth Any-
thing V2 at native resolution differs by 0.10–0.17%, and
Base and Large at full resolution by 0.19% and 0.25%
(median relative depth difference). Depth Anything V2-
Small at full resolution differs by 17.5%, and Depth Pro
by 1.9% (with a 1.6◦shift of its field-of-view estimate).
For these two we report accuracy from FP32 and speed
from FP16, which favours them. The FP32 Small model
is itself inaccurate at this resolution (57.7% AbsRel), so
the FP16 error is not the cause of its poor result.

are correct, and ONNX Runtime reproduces PyTorch to
within 0.002%. First, the attention pattern that PyTorch
exports from scaled_dot_product_attention (queries
and keys each scaled by the square root of the scale factor)
produced a wrong engine; exporting the same computa-
tion as softmax(q s k⊤) v fixed it.
